column1: # term|settled sense|warning
accuracy|Closeness of a measurement to the accepted true value.|Distinct from the agreement of repeated measurements.
precision|How closely repeated measurements agree.|Repeated readings may agree while sharing a bias.
uncertainty|A stated interval around a measured value within which the true value is expected.|It is not a known correction to the reading.
random error|Unpredictable variation that scatters repeated readings.|Averaging can reduce its effect.
systematic error|A consistent bias introduced by the instrument or method.|Repeated readings alone do not remove it.
independent variable|The quantity deliberately changed in an investigation.|Place it on the horizontal axis when constructing the required graph.
dependent variable|The quantity measured as the response to a deliberate change.|Place it on the vertical axis in the usual experimental graph.
control variable|A quantity held fixed so that the comparison tests the intended change.|Name the quantity and how it is kept fixed.
gradient|Vertical-axis change divided by horizontal-axis change for the chosen line.|Its physical meaning and unit follow from the actual axes.
scalar|A quantity described by magnitude without direction.|Speed and distance are scalar quantities.
vector|A quantity requiring magnitude and direction.|Keep the sign convention when adding collinear vectors.
distance|The length of the path travelled.|It is not necessarily the magnitude of displacement.
displacement|The directed change in position from start to finish.|Wave displacement instead means displacement from equilibrium.
speed|Distance travelled per elapsed time.|Whole-journey average speed uses total distance and total time.
velocity|Rate of change of displacement, with direction.|Average velocity depends on the net displacement.
acceleration|Rate of change of velocity.|A negative value is defined by the chosen positive direction.
resultant force|The single force equivalent to the vector sum of the forces.|Balanced forces can be present when the resultant is zero.
momentum|Mass multiplied by velocity.|Conservation of a system's total requires no external resultant force.
mass|A measure of the matter in an object.|It is not a force and is measured in kilograms.
weight|The gravitational force on an object, equal to its mass times gravitational field strength.|Its value can change while mass stays fixed.
inertia|The resistance of an object's motion to change, associated with its mass.|It is not an extra force acting on the object.
density|Mass per volume.|A volume-against-mass slope is reciprocal density.
moment|Turning effect measured by force times perpendicular lever arm.|Use instant for a time; do not confuse moment with momentum.
work|Energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement in its direction.|Its distance differs from the perpendicular lever arm in a moment.
power|Energy transferred or work done per time.|Qualify a mathematical power of ten explicitly.
pressure|Perpendicular force per area.|Area conversions require squared scale factors.
efficiency|Useful output energy divided by total input energy, usually expressed as a percentage.|Specify the intended useful output.
heat capacity|Energy needed to raise an object's temperature by one kelvin.|This is for the whole object, not a unit mass.
specific heat capacity|Energy per kilogram needed for a one-kelvin temperature rise.|It concerns a temperature change within a phase.
latent heat|Energy exchanged during a change of phase with unchanged temperature.|The syllabus uses this for a quantity of energy, not automatically per kilogram.
specific latent heat|Energy per kilogram for a phase change at unchanged temperature.|Include the unit-mass condition.
conduction|Thermal transfer through matter without bulk transport of that matter.|Electron transfer contributes in metals; do not describe convection instead.
convection|Thermal transport with bulk movement of a fluid, commonly driven by density differences.|State the physical movement, not just that heat rises.
thermal radiation|Transfer of energy by electromagnetic radiation.|It can occur without a material medium.
frequency|Number of complete cycles per unit time.|It is the reciprocal of period.
period|Time for one complete cycle.|Convert milliseconds before obtaining frequency in hertz.
wavelength|Distance between adjacent points in equal phase along a wave.|It is distinct from amplitude.
amplitude|Maximum magnitude of displacement from equilibrium.|For sound, it is linked to loudness rather than pitch.
wavefront|A line joining neighbouring points in equal phase.|A wavefront and the direction of propagation are different representations.
refraction|A direction change associated with a change of propagation medium and speed.|Angles are measured from the normal.
real image|An image formed by rays that actually converge.|It can be received on a suitably placed screen.
virtual image|An image located using backward extensions of divergent rays.|The rays do not actually converge at that location.
electric current|Rate of transfer of electric charge.|Conventional current is opposite electron drift in a metal.
electromotive force|Energy transferred by a source per charge driven around the circuit.|Distinguish the source's transfer from an individual component's transfer.
potential difference|Energy transferred in a component per charge passing through it.|Use volts, equivalent to joules per coulomb.
electrical resistance|Potential difference across a component divided by the current through it.|Air resistance is a drag force, a different meaning.
Ohm's law|Current is proportional to potential difference for a conductor whose temperature remains fixed.|A hot filament does not generally have constant resistance.
ferrous|Containing iron.|Do not use it as a substitute for a precise statement about every material's magnetic response.
isotope|Atoms of one element with equal proton numbers and unequal nucleon numbers.|The neutron numbers differ; the element is unchanged.
proton number|The number of protons in the nucleus.|It identifies the chemical element.
nucleon number|The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.|It is not the neutron number alone.
radioactive decay|Spontaneous change of an unstable nucleus with emission of radiation.|Individual emissions are random.
half-life|Time required for half the undecayed radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.|Apply successive halvings, not repeated subtraction of half the original sample.
